lessons.title: Normalize, then route
lessons.why: Routes match the number after the dial plan. A perfect route that expects E.164 will never see a local habit.
body: The person dials 020 7555 4010 or 425 555 0100. The first matching normalization rule rewrites it. Later rules do not run. The voice route then sees the result, usually E.164.

Put emergency short codes above any catch-all. A rule that turns every three-digit string into an extension will eat 999. Test the raw digits and the normalized form. The route is not wrong just because you typed the raw digits into it.

chart.title: Order
chart.note: You cannot route before you normalize.

lessons.say: First matching normalization rule wins. I test the route with the normalized number.
lessons.fault: A catch-all rule is first, so the emergency rule never runs.
lessons.listen: Normalize first, first match wins, then let the voice route see E.164.

lessons.title: Dial plans and first match
lessons.why: A branch that dials differently needs its own plan. Editing the global plan does not change a user who has a more specific one.
body: Tenant dial plans hold the rules. Grant the plan to the users it describes. A user with a specific plan will not pick up your edit to the global plan.

Keep rules anchored. A pattern without an end anchor will match a prefix of a longer number and translate the wrong thing. The lab on this campus is a teaching matcher with the same first-match idea, not the Microsoft service.
lessons.say: Specific rules first, grant the plan to the user, test as that user.
lessons.fault: You edit Global and the branch plan still has the old rule.
lessons.listen: Grant a dial plan to the user who needs it. First match wins, so emergency and specific rules go first.

lessons.title: PSTN usages are the permission
lessons.why: A route without a usage on the user’s policy is invisible. A usage on the wrong policy is an international bill.
body: PSTN usages are names. Voice routes attach to them. The user’s voice routing policy lists the usages in order. Teams walks that order. This campus’s matcher does the same and says so on the lab.
Give a branch a policy whose usages stop at national. Give headquarters a policy that continues to international. Do not share one policy and hope the route patterns save you.
lessons.say: The usage is the permission. The policy is the ordered list of permissions on the user.
lessons.fault: International works at a branch because that usage was left on the policy.
lessons.listen: PSTN usages are how a policy allows a route. Walk them in order.

lessons.title: Voice routes and gateways
lessons.why: The route is a regular expression plus an ordered list of SBCs. CUCM wildcards will not work here.
body: Anchor the pattern to the normalized number. List gateways with priorities. In this campus, priority 1 is tried first. Confirm the current article before you depend on a production tie-break. A second gateway that has never carried a call is a drawing.
Unassigned numbers you own should be treated on purpose, usually toward an attendant. A ported block with fifty silent numbers looks like an outage.
lessons.say: The voice route is a regex and a gateway list. I rehearse failover.
lessons.fault: Both SBCs are priority 1 and nobody knows which one took the call.
lessons.listen: A voice route matches the normalized number and tries gateways in priority order. Rehearse the second one.

lessons.title: A London worked example
lessons.why: One concrete walk is worth a page of definitions.
body: A London user dials a UK national number. Their dial plan emits +44. Their policy lists emergency, then UK national, then international. The UK route matches +44 and prefers sbc-lon, with sbc-man as priority 2. A Manchester-only policy has no international usage, so a US number fails closed.

An emergency 999 hits a rule that rewrites it to the emergency route, not to an extension and not to the international gateway. If you cannot tell that story with your own site names, you are not ready to change production.

lessons.title: Islands mode and other hard stops
lessons.why: Some failures are not routing tweaks. They are unsupported states.
body: Direct Routing is not supported in Islands mode. An SBC FQDN on onmicrosoft.com is not supported. A private CA is not a production certificate. AMR-WB is not a bypass codec. Media cannot be re-targeted mid-call.
Memorize the hard stops. They save you from debugging a dial plan that was never going to run.

chart.title: Hard stops
